debate_title: Should AI developers be legally liable for harms caused b...

conflicts.point: Whether upstream foundation model developers should be held under strict liability for downstream harms or if liability should rest at the deployment boundary.

positions.stance: Strict upstream liability forces developers of general-purpose optimization engines to internalize safety costs and prevents accountability vacuums.
Liability should focus on deployers who possess local context, while upstream strict liability creates uninsurable compliance moats that harm open-source developers.

conflicts.point: Whether compute-based regulatory thresholds (such as 10^26 FLOPs) effectively target systemic risk without creating protective moats for cloud incumbents.

positions.stance: Compute thresholds separate high-consequence foundational models from minor research checkpoints and allow targeted safety oversight.
Compute thresholds fail because algorithmic distillation allows sub-threshold models to match frontier capabilities, and static caps disadvantage new entrants.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream foundation model developers should face strict liability for downstream harms or if liability should rest at the deployment boundary.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist argument is stronger because base models remain inert until downstream actors provision compute and apply task-specific fine-tuning. Holding upstream developers strictly liable for every downstream application creates an uninsurable compliance burden that would likely crush open-source development and small market entrants.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical proof that base model weights possess inherent, uncontrollable hazard profiles that manifest identically across all downstream deployments regardless of user fine-tuning would flip this verdict.

verdicts.conflict: Whether compute-based regulatory thresholds effectively target systemic risk without creating protective moats for cloud incumbents.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic argument is stronger because algorithmic distillation and hardware efficiency gains allow sub-threshold models to match prior-generation frontier capabilities at a fraction of the cost. Static numeric caps like 10^26 FLOPs fail as administrative tools and function primarily as protective moats for large cloud providers.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that training compute correlates permanently with frontier capabilities and cannot be bypassed by architectural efficiencies would validate the compute threshold approach.

concepts.text: Drawing a bright-line regulatory boundary at 10^26 FLOPs turns training compute into a protective moat for incumbent cloud providers while leaving downstream deployers completely unaccountable for documented present harm.
concepts.speaker: Skeptic

concepts.text: When a healthcare provider in Ohio integrates a fine-tuned, sub-threshold model with 10^25 training FLOPs into its patient triage software, the resulting insurance denial or biased care allocation does not originate from the upstream developer's initial compute tally.
concepts.speaker: Skeptic

concepts.text: As tensor-processing units become faster and quantization techniques improve, the capability ceiling associated with 10^26 FLOPs shifts downward every year, meaning a model possessing frontier-grade optimization power next year will sit comfortably below the statutory trigger.
concepts.speaker: Skeptic
